Documentation of Main Micro Magic Tools

max

MAX is a full function IC Layout tool. MAX's features include:
  • Interactive viewing and editing of hierarchical layout
  • Continuous DRC feedback during layout
  • Hierarchical and incremental DRC
  • Hierarchical and incremental circuit extraction
  • Automatic generation of detailed parasitics and netlisting for critical paths
  • Interactive connectivity tracing
  • Interactive wiring tool with flylines to show connections not yet completed
  • Generators for layout structures, ranging from simple transistors and gates to large structures such as complete SRAMS
  • Interfaces to other tools, including schematic capture (for example Sue), and batch DRC and LVS (for example Dracula or ICRules).
  • Smart palette for easy control and feedback on layers
  • Integrated Postscript printing
  • Reads/writes GDSII, CIF, and Magic (.mag) in addition to native (.max) format
  • Full customization and extension via Tcl/Tk scripting language
  • Technology independence via technology description files
  • Optimized for large databases using load on demand
  • Optimized for Manhattan design, with support for arbitrary-angle data
  • Multi-platform, POSIX compliant C code, using Tcl/Tk for GUI interface

Documentation on MAX:

  • MAX Manual
  • MAX Text Commands
  • MAX Tutorial

mcc

The MegaCell Compiler (MCC) is a package that runs on top of MAX to build regular structures such as SRAMs, ROMs, PLAs, etc.

Documentation on MCC:

  • MCC Manual
  • MCC Tutorial
  • See also, the MAX Documentation

sue

Sue is a full featured "Schematic User Environment".

Documentation on Sue and the SUE Data Path Compiler (DPC):

  • Sue README
  • SUE Manual
  • SUE API Reference Guide
  • SUE Variables Reference Guide
  • SUE Tutorial
  • Sue FAQ

dpc

The Data Path Compiler (DPC) is a package that runs on top of SUE to build and analyze high-speed data paths.

Documentation on DPC:

  • DPC Manual
  • DPC Tutorial
  • See also, the Sue Documentation

nst

Nst (New Spice Tool) is a utility program for viewing waveforms generated by programs like HSPICE. It is designed for use with a schematic front-end such as Sue.

Documentation on Nst:

  • NST User's Manual
  • See also, the Sue Documentation

Installation

Installation of Micro Magic Tools

Installation of Micro Magic releases is quite simple: just "untar" the release into a directory of your choice. In addition each (would be) user must set one or two environment variables and include the correct bin directory in their path. This is usually done in their .login and .cshrc files.

Documentation on installation:

  • MMI Release README

Additional Documentation

extcheck

Extcheck checks the hierarchical ".ext" format generated by the MAX circuit extractor (netlister) for global connectivity and gives statistics on the total number of fets, nodes, etc.

Documentation on Extcheck:

  • Extcheck Man Page
  • Ext Format

ext2sim

Ext2sim converts the hierarchical ".ext" format generated by the MAX circuit extractor (netlister) to the flat ".sim" format used by a number of circuit simulators.

Documentation on Ext2sim:

  • Ext2sim Man Page
  • Extcheck Man Page (documents some common command line options)
  • Ext Format
  • Sim Format

ext2spice

Ext2spice converts the hierarchical ".ext" format generated by the MAX circuit extractor (netlister) to spice format.

Documentation on Ext2spice:

  • Ext2spice Man Page
  • Extcheck Man Page (documents some common command line options)
  • Ext Format

gemini

Gemini compares two netlists in ".sim" format. Documentation on Ext2spice:
  • Gemini Man Page
  • Gemini User's Manual (in postscript form)
  • Sim Format

mmidoc

Mmidoc brings up complete documentation on the Micro Magic tools in Netscape (or your favorite web browser).

Documentation on Mmidoc:

  • Mmidoc README

mmi_tutorial

mmi_tutorial brings up a popup that allows you to install, view, and/or print the MMI MAX, MCC, SUE, or DPC tutorials. To run, just type mmi_tutorial at any unix prompt.

mmi_tclsh

Mmi_tclsh is a version of Tclsh that does not depend on Tcl being installed on your system: it uses the Tcl library in ${MMI_TOOLS}/lib/. It also includes special Micro Magic extensions.

Documentation on Mmi_Tclsh:

    Tcl/Tk documentation

mmi_tclsh

Mmi_wish is a version of Wish that does not depend on Tcl/Tk being installed on your system: it uses the libraries in ${MMI_TOOLS}/lib/. It also includes special Micro Magic extensions.

Documentation on Mmi_wish:

    Tcl/Tk documentation

Tcl/Tk

The MMI tools use embedded Tcl/Tk. This provides:
  • A complete (and consistent) scripting language for each tool.
  • A toolkit for GUI extensions.
  • A powerful mechanism for interaction between tools.
  • Portability between platforms.
Documentation on Tcl/Tk:
  • http://www.scriptics.com (the official Tcl/Tk website)
  • Tcl and the Tk Toolkit", authored by John Ousterhout, published by Addison-Weseley.

Sue to edif converter (sue2edif)

    "sue2edif" is a plug-in addition to Sue for writing an EDIF design file based on the current design loaded in Sue.

    Installation

    To install the EDIF writer, you need to add the following line to your .suerc file: 

            menu_add -menu file -label "Write EDIF" -command edif_write -position 10 \
	         -help "Writes the EDIF for the given schematic and descendents."
    Typically, this line is added to the site-wide .suerc file in $MMI_TOOLS/../mmi_local/sue/.suerc, so that all users can access it. The .suerc file in mmi_local.sample provided with the release includes this line commented out. You need only uncomment it.

    When the tool has been properly installed, a new command "Write EDIF" will appear in the the Sue "File" menu.

    Operation

    Display the schematic view of the top-level cell of the design file to be written.

    Click on the "Write EDIF" command in the "File" menu.

    The display will be seen to cycle through heirarchically included components of the current design. Progress messages are displayed on the console.

    When the command is complete with no errors, the console displays the message "done". the output EDIF file is written to the same directory as the top cell but with the ".edif" extension.

    Output

    The EDIF file is a correct representation according to Version 2 0 0, published as "EIA Recommended Standard EIA-548-1988", dated March 14, 1988. Only "level 0" constructs are used.

    The file written is an EDIF representation of the design selected. Each SUE cell called for in the design appears as a "cell" definition in the EDIF file. All the cells are organized into a single EDIF library within the file.

    Cells are written for all constructs, includeing library components such as transistors and informational constructs such as title bars, so the complete design as it appears in SUE will be available to be imported into whatever other CAD tool.

    The output file will be accurately read by the MMI EDIF conversion tool "edif2sue". The resulting set of SUE files reconstructs the original design. The correct operation of readers for other CAD tools is obviously beyond our control, but we would like to hear about difficulties and are willing to try to "make it work".

    A note on nets

    EDIF contains redundant information describing nets; there is logical connectivity information in "joined" expressions, and there is graphical information in "display" expressions.

    SUE uses the graphical information to construct its internal representation of the design, so "what you see is what you get." In other tools this may not be true, and discrepancies between the connectivity and graphical information may cause unpredictable problems.

    The generated EDIF file contains correct connectivity information.

    In some cases a "name_net_s" component is used to select a subset of wires from a bus. EDIF has no way of representing this kind of construction directly, so what the tool does is create separate "joined" statements for each bit of buses which are "split" in this way. These individual nets have names like "bit[3]" and contain a joined statement that lists the one-bit-wide ports connected by this net; there is no graphical information. There is also a net with a name like "bit[7:0]" which contains the graphical information for all bits of the net, but no explicit connectivity information. The name_net_s's appear as distinct instances in the ordinary way.

    If there is a problem with importing the generated EDIF file into other CAD tools, this is likely where it will be, due to the basic incompatiblity of the various representations.

verilog_to_sue

    Verilog_to_sue translates a hierarchical verilog netlist into hierarchical sue schematics. It only translates structural netlists and will report warnings on modules that contain behavioral verilog.

    Usage:

    To execute verilog_to_sue, type the following at a unix prompt: 
            verilog_to_sue *.v
    verilog_to_sue reads each of the verilog files (*.v) and generates a foo.sue file for every module foo it finds in the verilog files. You then simply load these .sue files like you would load any other .sue files.

    All purely structural modules are translated into sue schematics and icons. The icons are rectangles with inputs and inouts on the left and outputs on the right. Schematics contain inputs and inouts on the left and outputs on the right. A matrix of icons and bus combines go in between. The icons are for instantiated modules. The bus combines are for verilog assigns, and for concatenations on instantiation ports.

    A module with any behavioral code is translated into a schematic with the words "behavioral module". The structural code is not translated in a module of mixed behavioral and structural code.

    Installation:

    If you've done a standard MMI install, then verilog_to_sue should already be in your $path. Here are the relevant files: 

            $MMI_TOOLS/bin.<your machine type>/verilog_to_sue
	        link to $MMI_TOOLS/scripts/verilog_to_sue

        $MMI_TOOLS/bin.<your machine type>/verilog_preprocessor
	        link to $MMI_TOOLS/scripts/verilog_preprocessor

        $MMI_TOOLS/bin.<your machine type>/verilog_parser
    	        binary for verilog parser

        $MMI_TOOLS/scripts/verilog_to_sue
	        script for verilog_to_sue

        $MMI_TOOLS/scripts/verilog_preprocessor
	        script for verilog preprocessor
    We've assumed you have perl in /usr/local/bin/perl. If you have it somewhere else, you need to go into $MMI_TOOLS/scripts and change the path of each of the scripts that has "#!/usr/local/bin/perl" in the first line. Or you can move perl to /usr/local/bin/perl, or put a link there to wherever you have it. If you don't have perl at all, then you need to get it.

    Note: verilog_to_sue requires perl5.0 or later.
